title: Preventing Falls With Guardrails
summary: Falls are a leading cause of construction deaths. Guardrails stop falls from edges, roofs, and platforms. This talk covers where guardrails are required and the 42-inch height rule.
talking_points: Your employer must train every worker to recognize fall hazards and use fall protection.
Guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall-arrest systems must be in place wherever there is a fall risk.
Guardrails are required on work surfaces where workers could fall more than 6 feet.
Top rails must be 42 inches high, plus or minus 3 inches, with a mid-rail in between.
When guardrails cannot be used, wear a body harness with a lanyard tied to a secure anchor point provided by your employer.
site_hazards_to_check: Open edges, platforms, or roofs with falls over 6 feet and no guardrail
Top rails outside the 42-inch, plus or minus 3-inch, range
Missing mid-rails or damaged, loose guardrail sections
Guardrail removed for access and not replaced
No anchor points or harnesses where guardrails are not feasible
discussion_questions: Where on this site could someone fall more than 6 feet today?
How do you check that a guardrail is at the right height and strength?
What is your backup if a guardrail has to come down for material handling?

flags: OSHA mapping and tolerances verified accurate: 29 CFR 1926.501 (fall protection duty), 1926.502 (systems criteria), 1926.503 (training). Top rail 42 in plus or minus 3 in (1926.502(b)(1)); 6 ft fall-height trigger for construction (1926.501(b)(1)); midrail when there is no wall/structural member at least 21 in high (1926.502(b)(2)).

Non-blocking enhancement: a discussion question asks how to check guardrail 'strength' but no talking point states the 1926.502(b)(3)-(5) load criteria (200 lb outward/downward on the top rail, 150 lb on the midrail); consider adding.
